candidates.title: Prepare game-test CSV rows for review

demandEvidence.chore: A mobile game tester records battery, temperature, frame drops and notes, exports a CSV, and pastes it into a Google Sheet; file triggers sometimes fail or duplicate processing.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Right now I type it into a notes app during the session, then later export a CSV from that app and paste it into a Google Sheet.

ease.reason: The CSV extraction and duplicate-removal docs support a small file-in, row-out prototype; phone intake is not documented.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: independent game testers or small QA teams may pay for cleaner log preparation; this post shows no purchase intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week CSV prototype can extract rows and compare chosen keys using the supplied n8n docs; reliable mobile uploads and correct matching fields remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: Documented extraction and duplicate checks automate repeatable file handling, but a tester must upload files, select comparison fields, and review records.

evidence.reason: The retained spans state the measurements, later CSV export and sheet paste, and missed or repeated triggers; this is one post without corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A reviewable table of extracted game-test rows with likely duplicate rows flagged for a tester to inspect.
inputs: A synthetic CSV containing session time, device, battery, temperature, frame-drop count and note
A tester-selected set of fields to compare when identifying likely repeats
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator manually supplies a completed CSV file for one review run.
steps: Extract the supplied CSV into row records.
Check that required test columns are present and flag missing values.
Compare rows using the operator-selected fields.
Mark matching rows as possible repeats without deleting them.
Produce a review table and a short count of flagged rows.
Have the tester verify all flags before using or importing any row.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a synthetic file with labeled required fields and known repeated rows, verify that extraction preserves each supplied value and that only rows matching the selected comparison fields are flagged.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The tester supplies and checks the CSV, chooses fields that define a duplicate, verifies flagged rows, and handles any live upload or sheet import; the prototype must not silently discard records.
unverified: Whether the real exported CSV has stable headers and identifiers
Whether chosen comparison fields distinguish repeated measurements from legitimate similar rows
Whether phone uploads finish before an n8n trigger reads the file
Whether the proposed service is useful or anyone would pay for it

candidates.reason: The task is concrete and the attached n8n references support CSV extraction and duplicate comparisons, so it receives a scoped assessment. Its provisional mean is 5.4, below six; live intake, a correct duplicate contract, and buyer demand remain unresolved.

candidates.title: Compare daily Shopify purchase exports

demandEvidence.chore: Export daily Shopify online-store orders and Meta purchases for the same 30-day period, then compare the totals to investigate gaps or duplicate tracking.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: In Shopify, export daily orders for the same 30 days, Online Store channel only, without test and cancelled orders.

ease.reason: A beginner can compare two operator-supplied daily export tables; the attached instructions describe their filters but no software capability supports the comparison.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small ecommerce advertisers may pay for faster discrepancy review; the how-to post does not establish purchase intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic comparison of supplied daily totals is bounded, while export automation, attribution interpretation and diagnosing a live pixel remain unsupported.

autonomy.reason: A proposed table comparison can flag mismatched dates, but a person must export both sources, inspect attribution differences and investigate any tracking cause.

evidence.reason: The retained instructions specify both exports and explain ordinary attribution gaps and one possible duplicate-tracking pattern; no recurring buyer demand is corroborated.

experimentPlan.output: A dated comparison table that flags differing supplied purchase totals and lists possible explanations for human review.
inputs: Synthetic daily Shopify order totals with channel and test/cancelled-order labels
Synthetic daily Meta purchase totals labeled with the selected attribution window
An operator-supplied date range and column mapping
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator manually provides two matching date-range tables for a review run.
steps: Check that both tables cover the same dates.
Apply the supplied channel, test-order and attribution labels.
Compare totals by date and mark mismatches.
Show the comparison with a neutral note that attribution methods can differ.
Flag patterns for investigation without diagnosing their cause.
Have a merchant verify the exports and inspect tracking settings independently.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a synthetic pair of tables with known dates and totals, confirm that aligned dates are compared correctly, mismatched totals are marked, and the output does not label a difference as a duplicate sale without human verification.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A merchant exports and maps both tables, confirms filters and attribution settings, investigates any flagged date, and decides whether tracking needs changes; the prototype does not access a store or alter tracking.
unverified: Whether real export headers and date formats are consistent
Whether manual comparison is a recurring burden for a defined merchant group
Whether flags help distinguish ordinary attribution differences from tracking errors
Whether any merchant would pay for this review

candidates.reason: The source supplies a detailed manual export and comparison task, so a bounded experiment is assessed. Its provisional mean is 5.2, below six: the evidence is one instructional post, with no implementation reference, repeated customer demand, or supported live integration.
